rounds.proof_sketch: The kernel is launched with `dim3 grid(batch_size)` where batch_size=128. CUDA guarantees blockIdx.x ∈ [0, batch_size-1] = [0, 127]. Original condition `batch_idx >= 128` is always false. Mutated condition `batch_idx > 128` is also always false. Both conditions never trigger early return for any actual block index.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation changes the early-return guard from `batch_idx >= batch_size` to `batch_idx > batch_size`. Since the kernel is launched with exactly `batch_size` blocks (grid dimension = 128), the valid block indices range from 0 to 127. For all values in this range, both `batch_idx >= 128` and `batch_idx > 128` evaluate to false. The guard was defensive code protecting against out-of-bounds block indices, which can never occur given the fixed launch configuration. The mutation would only matter if `batch_idx` could equal `batch_size` (128), which is impossible when the grid size is exactly `batch_size`.
rounds.kill_strategy: Unkillable under fixed-shape contract. The mutation affects a guard condition that protects against out-of-bounds block indices, but CUDA launch semantics guarantee blockIdx.x < gridDim.x. Since grid.x = batch_size = 128, blockIdx.x is always in [0, 127], making both the original (>=) and mutated (>) conditions always evaluate to false.
rounds.recommendations: Guard conditions protecting against kernel launch parameter violations (like batch_idx >= batch_size when grid = batch_size) are fundamentally unreachable through value-level testing. Mutation testing tools should apply semantic analysis of CUDA launch configurations to filter out mutations to unreachable guards, or such guards could be refactored to use compile-time assertions or removed entirely when launch parameters are known to be correct.
